en: In the *Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa*, after non-duality— which was initially asserted on the basis of scripture by means of the determination of the syllable *Oṃ*— and which was further established through the falsity of the distinction between external objects, has been directly ascertained once more through both scripture and reasoning, the conclusion is made at the end that "this is the supreme truth."

The dualists and the nihilists are the adversaries of this non-dualistic vision which is the meaning of the traditional scripture; because their views are mutually contradictory, they serve as a locus for afflictions such as attachment and aversion, and thus their status as false views is indicated.
Since it is not a locus for afflictions, the non-dualistic vision is praised as the right view.

Therefore, having here demonstrated at length that [the various views] are not right views because they are mutually contradictory, the establishment of the non-dual (advaita) view must be concluded by way of negating them according to the logic of exclusion (*avīta-nyāya*); thus, the *Alātaśānti* is commenced.
In this regard, the first verse is intended as a salutation to the founder of the tradition of the non-dual view, by means of his very nature as non-duality.

For the fulfillment of one's intended purpose at the commencement of a treatise, the worship of the Teacher is indeed required. I pay homage to that Best of Bipeds, the Perfectly Awakened One, who, through knowledge equal to space and non-different from the object of knowledge, perceives all phenomena as being like the sky.
This is slightly incomplete like space, resembling space, equal to space;
by means of that knowledge which resembles space, what [does one perceive]?
The dharmas as being without self.
Of what kind? "Equal to the sky" (*gaganopama*): those whose comparison is the sky are "equal to the sky"; [he perceives] those qualities of his own self.
Furthermore, there is a qualification of knowledge itself: knowledge is non-different from the knowable qualities that constitute its own nature, like fire and heat, or like the sun and its light.

By means of that knowledge—which is non-different from the knowable, comparable to space, and inseparable from the essential nature of the knowable self—one [perceives] the qualities equal to the sky.

"He is the perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha), he has awakened perfectly"—this very one who is named Nārāyaṇa is the Lord (īśvara). I bow to him, I pay homage to him, the best among bipeds; the intention is that he is the most excellent, the foremost among men as characterized by being bipeds, the Supreme Person (puruṣottama). By means of this salutation to the Teacher, the vision of ultimate reality (paramārthadarśana), which is devoid of the distinctions of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, is what is intended to be established in this treatise; it was promised by way of refuting opposing views.
It comes to be. //1//
Now, for the purpose of praising the yoga of the non-dual vision, there is this salutation:
"The yoga known as 'the Untouchable' (asparśayoga) is indeed beneficial and brings happiness to all beings."
I bow to him who has taught that which is free from dispute and contradiction.
"Contact" (sparśa) means connection; that yoga with which there is no connection whatsoever at any time by anyone is the "untouchable yoga" (asparśayoga), whose very nature is Brahman.
The phrase "indeed, so-called" means that it is well-known among the knowers of Brahman as the "untouchable yoga.
And that is the happiness of all beings.
There may be something that, although distinguished by being a means to ultimate happiness, is nonetheless of the nature of suffering, such as ascetic penance;
but this [state] is not like that.
Rather, it is pleasant for all sentient beings.
Thus, while certain enjoyments of sense-objects here may be pleasant, they are not beneficial; this [state], however, is both pleasant and beneficial because its nature is eternally unshakable.

Furthermore, "non-contention" (avivāda) means that where there is no contention—contention being the speaking of contradictory words through the grasping of positions and counter-positions—that is non-contention.
Why? Because it is non-contradictory.
The meaning is: "I bow to," that is, "I prostrate before," that yoga which has been taught and expounded by the scripture in such a manner. //2//
START MandUpK 4.3 How do those who maintain duality contradict one another? It is said: For indeed, some proponents assert the birth of an existent entity.
Other wise ones, however, dispute with one another regarding that which has not come into being.

For indeed, some proponents—namely the Sāṃkhyas, and not all dualists—desire the birth or production of an entity that already exists; whereas others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, who are wise, intelligent, and conceited in their wisdom (the meaning being "those who pride themselves on their intellect"), dispute and speak in opposition, desiring to defeat one another. This is the intended sense. //3//
START MandUpK 4.4 By thus contradicting one another with their speech and refuting each other’s positions, what is being proclaimed? It is said:
"Nothing that exists is born; nothing that does not exist is born."
Thus disputing, they indeed proclaim non-duality and the absence of birth.

An exponent of non-existence (*asadvādī*), by stating that "an existing (*bhūta*) entity does not arise because it already exists, just like the Self (*ātman*)," refutes the Sāṃkhya position regarding the arising of the existent. Likewise, the Sāṃkhya, by stating that "a non-existent (*abhūta*) thing does not arise at all because it does not exist, just like a hare's horn," refutes the position of the proponent of non-existence regarding the arising of the non-existent. Though they speak in opposition, these non-dualists (*advayins*)—by mutually negating the positions of the arising of the existent and the non-existent—actually proclaim and reveal *ajāti*, which is non-arising.
They [are as follows]. //4//
We approve of the non-arising (ajāti) being proclaimed by them;
we do not dispute with them— understand this as being beyond dispute.
When they proclaim non-arising in this manner, we approve it, saying, "Let it be so," but we do not dispute with them by grasping at a thesis and a counter-thesis;
such is our intention regarding how they [speak] to one another.
Therefore, O disciples, understand that this very view which is without dispute, free from contention, and the vision of ultimate reality, has been accepted by us. //5//
Proponents of [theories of] arising desire the birth of a dharma that is itself unborn.
For how can a dharma that is unborn and immortal undergo mortality?
"All [schools] are proponents of both existence and non-existence"—this was the verse in the commentary composed previously. //6//
The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise does the immortal become mortal;
a transformation of nature (prakṛti) can never occur in any way whatsoever. (MandUpK 4.7)
For one whose dharma, being immortal by nature, undergoes mortality,
how can that which is made immortal remain unshakable?

The presentation here of these verses, whose meaning has already been stated, is for the purpose of demonstrating that the positions of opposing disputants are mutually contradictory and thus express approval of non-arising. //7-8//
START MandUpK 4.9 Since even the worldly primordial nature (*prakṛti*) does not undergo transformation, he asks: "What is it? and says:
That which is innate, natural, co-emergent, and uncreated—know that to be *prakṛti*, which does not abandon its own nature. (MandUk 4.9)
*Saṃsiddhi* is perfect accomplishment; that which arises from it is *sāṃsiddhikī*. For example, the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* by perfected yogins is their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
That nature does not change for those yogins even in the past or future times; it remains exactly as it is.
Likewise, there is the *svābhāvikī* [nature], which exists by the very nature of a substance, such as the characteristics of heat and light in fire and so forth.
That [nature] also does not deviate across different times or different places.
Likewise, there is that which is innate (*sahajā*), born together with the self itself, such as the characteristic of flying through the sky and so forth belonging to birds and the like.
There is also another kind which is uncreated by anyone (*akṛtā*), such as the characteristic of flowing toward lower ground belonging to water.
Whatever else there may be that does not abandon its own nature should be understood as "prakṛti" (nature) in the world.
Even among worldly objects falsely imagined, the nature does not become otherwise; how much more so in the case of ultimate realities whose nature is immortal? Such is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, what is the object of that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) whose transformation is imagined by the proponents [of other systems], or what is the fault in such an imagination? To this he says:
"All phenomena (*dharma*) are by their very nature free from old age and death; those who desire old age and death fall away through that misconception. (MandUpK 4.10)
"Free from old age and death"—the meaning is that they are devoid of all transformations such as old age, death, and so forth.
Who? All phenomena (*dharmas*), all selves (*ātman*); this is by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and primordial essence (*prakṛti*).

Being of such a nature, while desiring—almost as if desiring—old age and death for phenomena, they imagine them within themselves like a snake in a rope; thus they "fall," which means they deviate from their own intrinsic nature.
The meaning is: by means of the thought of that [world], namely the anxiety regarding birth and death; that is, by the fault of being permeated by the state of being that [world]. //10//

START MandUpK 4.11 The Vaiśeṣika asks: How can it be said by the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain the doctrine of pre-existent origination (*sajjātivāda*), that [the effect] is unproduced? He says: "For one for whom the effect is indeed the cause, the cause is born from that [effect]."
How can that which is being born be unborn, and how can it be both differentiated and eternal?

The meaning is this: for whichever proponent the cause is characterized by having a subtle substrate (*mṛdvad-upādāna-lakṣaṇa*), and for whom the effect is simply the cause itself transforming into the form of the effect—for that proponent, the unborn *pradhāna* and so forth, being existent, is born in the form of effects such as the *mahat* and so on.

But if the *pradhāna*, while being born in the form of the *mahat* and so forth, is called "unborn," how can that be? For they [the proponents] contradict themselves by asserting both "it is born" and "it is unborn."
Furthermore, they assert that *pradhāna* is eternal; however, the meaning is: how could it be eternal if it is divided, split, or cracked in one part?
For in the world, things with parts, such as a jar, which possess the property of being cracked in one part, are never seen to be eternal.
The intention is that they are propounding a contradiction, namely that something is both "unborn" (and thus eternal) and yet "split in one part. //11//
To clarify the very point already stated, he says:
"If there is non-difference from the cause, then the effect is unborn."
For how can your cause be established as permanent on the basis of an effect that is itself born?

If you maintain that the effect is non-different from the unborn cause, then it follows that the effect is itself unborn. Furthermore, this other contradiction arises for you: that the effect is both "effect" and "unborn.
Moreover, if the effect and the cause are non-different, how could the cause—which is non-different from the effect that is being born—be eternal and permanent?
For indeed, one part of a hen is cooked while another part is reserved for laying eggs. //12//
Furthermore:
"For one who holds that what is born arises from the unborn, there is indeed no illustrative example."
Furthermore, it would follow that there is no fixed order between what has already been born and what is being born.
For that proponent for whom an effect arises from an unborn, unproduced entity, there is indeed no example.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of an example, it follows by implication that nothing whatsoever is born from the unborn; this is what is established.

Furthermore, when one accepts that an entity being produced arises from something already born, then that [born thing] must arise from another, and that too from another—thus, an infinite regress (anavasthā) results.
The meaning is that there would be an infinite regress. //13//
START MandUpK 4.14:

Relying on that which has been stated by the Śruti— namely, “But where everything has become the Self alone for him” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14)— which signifies the non-existence of duality from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says:
For those for whom the cause has a beginning and the effect has a beginning,
how can they describe the cause and the effect as being without beginning?
For those proponents for whom the "beginning" (ādi) of causes such as dharma and so forth is the body and its aggregates—

that is, the cause is the beginning— and likewise, for whom the cause is the beginning while the fruit, namely the aggregate of the body and so forth, has dharma, adharma, and so on as its beginning; how can the beginninglessness of both cause and fruit be described by those very people who assert that cause and fruit possess a beginning through their mutual relationship of effect and cause?
The meaning is that it is contradictory;
for it is not possible for the eternal, immutable Self to possess the nature of cause and effect. //14//
START MandUpK 4.15 It is explained how they accept what is contradictory: "For those [who hold this view], the cause is the beginning of the effects, and the effect is the beginning of the cause."
In that way, their birth would be like the birth of a son from a father.
For those who assert that the birth of a cause occurs from a fruit that is itself produced by that very cause, such a contradiction is stated as being like the birth of a father from his son. //15//
START MandUpK 4.16 If you think that the aforementioned contradiction is not tenable to accept— then you must admit a sequence between cause and effect when they are possible.
Because if they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no connection between them, like [two] horns.
In the case of the occurrence—that is, the arising—of cause and effect, you must accept this sequence:
the cause first and the effect afterwards.
Furthermore, if they were to occur simultaneously, there would be no relationship between cause and effect by way of being the producer and the produced.
Just as in the case of the left and right horns of a cow, which cannot exist simultaneously. //16//
START MandUpK 4.17 How is there no connection? To this he says: Being produced from the fruit, your cause is not established.
How can a cause that is unestablished produce an effect?
A cause that is arising from an effect that has not yet attained its own nature and is thus non-existent—like a rabbit's horn—is not established; it does not undergo birth.
How will that which has not attained its own nature and is unestablished, being a mere conceptualization like a rabbit's horn, produce an effect for you?
Indeed, a relationship of cause and effect is never observed between two things that are mutually dependent for their establishment and are both like the horns of a rabbit.
The intended meaning is "or otherwise. //17//

If the establishment of the cause depends on the effect, and the establishment of the effect depends on the cause, which of the two is established first, such that the other could be established in dependence upon it?

Even though the causal relationship between cause and effect has been refuted by the fault of their lack of connection, if you nevertheless maintain that the mutual establishment of cause and effect is accepted, then tell me: which of the two, cause or effect, is established first, such that the subsequent one might be established in dependence upon that prior establishment? This is the meaning. //18//
START MandUpK 4.19 Now, if you think that this cannot be stated— [is it] incapacity, lack of understanding, or rather a violation of the sequence?
For in this way, non-arising has been fully elucidated by the Buddhas in every respect.
This means that it is incapacity, lack of thorough knowledge, non-discrimination of reality, and delusion.

Alternatively, this refers to the subversion, reversal, or alteration of the sequence you have described—namely, the establishment of the effect from the cause and the establishment of the cause from the effect, characterized by their mutual succession.

Thus, because the relationship of cause and effect between the cause and the effect is untenable, the non-arising and the non-origination of everything has been fully elucidated and revealed by the wise ones—the Buddhas—who speak of the faults inherent in each other's positions. This is the meaning.
START MandUpK 4.20:

"But surely we have stated that the relation between cause and effect exists between the cause and its dissolution; this [objection] you have raised—such as 'like the birth of a father from a son' or 'like a horn, there is no connection,' and so forth—is merely a verbal quibble (*śabda-cchala*) based on mere words."
For we do not accept that the establishment of the effect is from an unestablished cause, nor that the establishment of the cause is from an unestablished effect.
What then? We accept the relationship of cause and effect as being like that of a seed and a sprout.
To this, it is said:
The example known as the seed and the sprout is always equivalent to the point to be proven;
for a reason that is equivalent to the point to be proven is not suitable for establishing that which is to be proven.
My intention is that the example known as the seed and the sprout is equivalent to the point to be proven (the *sādhya*).
[Objection: But is not the causal relationship between the seed and the sprout directly perceived and beginningless (*anādi*)?
[Reply: No, because it is admitted that each preceding [cause] has a beginning, just like its successor.
Just as this present other sprout that has arisen is preceded by a seed, and that other seed is preceded by yet another sprout—thus, because they arise in a sequence, they possess a beginning;

so too, each preceding sprout and each preceding seed likewise possesses a beginning. Since every instance of the seed-and-sprout series possesses a beginning individually, it is impossible for anything therein to be beginningless. The same applies to causes and effects.
If it is argued that the continuum of seed and sprout is beginningless, we say no, because unity is untenable.

For those who maintain its beginninglessness do not admit a single entity called a "continuum of seed and sprout" distinct from the seeds and sprouts themselves, nor a "continuum of cause and effect. Therefore, it is well said that there is no beginning for either the cause or the fruit.
How is it described by them?
The intention is that even other [fallacies] are not "quibbling" (chala) because they are logically untenable.

Furthermore, the meaning is that those skilled in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) do not employ a reason that is equivalent to the probandum (sādhyasama) as a basis for establishing the probandum in worldly practice.
By "reason" (hetu), an example (dṛṣṭānta) is intended here, because it is that which makes [the matter] understood;
for what is under discussion is the example, not the reason. //20//
START MandUpK 4.21:
To explain how non-arising is elucidated by the Buddhas, he says: "The lack of cognition of before and after is the elucidation of non-arising."
For how could that which is prior to the dharma that is being born be perceived?
This lack of prior knowledge regarding the sequence of cause and effect is what illuminates and makes known the state of non-arising; this is the meaning.
For if a phenomenon is apprehended as it is arising, why is its cause not apprehended prior to it?

Necessarily, by one who perceives that which is being produced, its producer must also be perceived, because the relationship between the produced and the producer is inseparable. Therefore, the meaning is that this [argument] merely illustrates non-origination. //21//
Furthermore, for this reason nothing whatsoever is born, because that entity which is being born—
Not any entity whatsoever is born from itself, nor from another, nor from both; not any entity whatsoever is born that is existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent.
Neither from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor as existent, nor as non-existent, nor as both existent and non-existent is it born; its birth is not possible in any manner whatsoever.
First of all, it does not arise from itself—that is, from its own unestablished nature—just as a pot does not arise from that very same pot.
Nor does it arise from another, that is, from something else, just as a cloth arises from a pot, or one cloth from another cloth.
Likewise, it does not arise from both, because of contradiction; just as a jar or a cloth is not produced from both a jar and a cloth.
But surely, a jar is produced from clay, and a son from a father?
It is true that for the ignorant there exists the notion and the word "it is born.
However, those who possess discernment examine those very words and notions to determine whether they are real or false.
Upon such examination, the object of those words and notions—namely, things characterized as jars, sons, and so forth—is found to be nothing but the word itself.
This is because of the Vedic scripture (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4): "It is a mere modification based on speech.
If it exists, it is not born because of its existence, like clay or a father;
if it does not exist, it likewise is not born precisely because of its non-existence, like the horn of a hare.
Furthermore, neither an existent nor a non-existent thing is produced, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess contradictory properties.
Therefore, it is established that no entity whatsoever is produced.
As for those who maintain that the very act of arising is what is "produced," thereby accepting the identity of action, agent, and result, as well as the momentariness of entities—

These [theories] are already set aside from afar, because [the object] does not persist for even a moment beyond the instant of determining "this is such-and-such," and because memory is impossible for that which has not been experienced. //22//
Furthermore, by you who accept that cause and effect are beginningless, you would necessarily be accepting that cause and effect are actually unborn.
How so?
A cause does not arise from that which is beginningless, nor does a fruit [arise] by way of its own nature;
for that which has no beginning, indeed, has no beginning at all.
A cause is not produced from a beginningless effect that lacks a beginning;
for you do not accept the birth of a cause from an unarisen, beginningless effect.
Furthermore, it is not admitted that an effect arises without a cause from a beginningless, unborn cause that is by its very nature devoid of causal conditions.
Therefore, by you who accept beginninglessness, the non-arising of cause and effect must be accepted;
for in this world, that which has no beginning—that is, no cause—does not possess the aforementioned "birth" as its beginning.
Indeed, a beginning is accepted only for that which possesses a cause, not for that which lacks a cause. (23)
Desiring to further strengthen the very point already stated, he raises an objection once more:
"The designation must have a cause; otherwise, there would be the destruction of the duality."
And because defilement is perceived, the existence of the dependent nature is accepted.

Cognition is conceptual designation (*prajñapti*), which is the perception of sound and so forth; its "having a cause" (*sanimittatva*) means having a basis (*nimitta*), a cause (*kāraṇa*), or an object (*viṣaya*). We maintain that this state of having a cause—that is, having an object—means having an object distinct from itself. For there can be no conceptual designation, such as the perception of sound and so forth, that is devoid of an object.
This is because it possesses a causal basis (*sanimitta*).

Otherwise, if it were devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*), it would follow that there is the destruction—meaning the non-existence—of the duality consisting of the variety of cognitions such as sound, touch, blue, yellow, red, and so forth.
Yet, there is no absence of this duality of the variety of cognitions, because it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣatvāt*).
Therefore, because of the observation of the two-fold variety of the [subjective] counter-correlate (*prati*),

the system of others— the *paratantra* (dependent nature)— is another treatise; it is held that this *paratantra*, which is based on the *paratantra* and consists of external objects distinct from cognition, does not exist.

For it is not possible for a designation (*prajñapti*), whose nature is mere manifestation, to possess variety through an intrinsic difference in its own-being (*svabhāva*) without the diversity of external objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
The intention is that, just as in the case of a crystal, variety is not possible without the support of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as blue;
thus, there exists an external object distinct from cognition which serves as the basis for the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) means that which causes defilement; it has the sense of suffering (*duḥkha*).
For suffering is indeed perceived as having fire, burning, and so forth as its cause.
If external factors such as fire, which serve as the cause for burning and so forth, did not exist apart from consciousness, then the suffering of burning and so forth would not be perceived.
However, it is indeed perceived;
therefore, we consider that there exists an external object.
For affliction is not logically possible within consciousness alone.
The intention is that [the rule] does not apply elsewhere, because it is not observed there. //24//
To this it is replied: The fact that designation has a cause is accepted because of the observation of logical reasoning.
The signlessness of the sign is accepted because of the vision of reality as it is.

"Very well; you maintain that designation (prajñapti) possesses a cause because of the observation of reasoning regarding the perception of the two-fold affliction. Now, remain firm for a moment on this point: that the observation of reasoning is the cause for accepting the suchness of the entity.
Tell me, what follows from that?"
It is said:

we maintain that the "signless" (animitta) nature—that is, the lack of being an object (*anālambanatva*) and the lack of being a cause for diversity—of signs such as jars, which are considered the objects of conceptual designation (*prajñapti*), is established through the vision of reality (*bhūtadarśana*), which is the vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārthadarśana*).
How so? Because it is the vision of reality; that is to say, the vision of the ultimate truth.
For a jar does not exist apart from the perception of its true nature as clay,

just as a buffalo or a cloth does not exist apart from a horse or its threads, nor do threads exist apart from their filaments; thus, the meaning is that upon perceiving each subsequent constituent element, we do not perceive any causal basis for the cessation of verbal designations.
Alternatively, it is intended that the external object is non-causal because it is seen as it truly is, just as the snake and so forth [are non-existent] in the case of a rope and so forth;
and because it is the object of erroneous perception, the causal sign (nimitta) would be non-causal.

Because it does not exist in their absence—indeed, for those who are in deep sleep, in meditative absorption, or liberated, no external object distinct from the self is perceived, since there is an absence of delusory vision.

For an object apprehended by a madman is not perceived as being of that same nature even by those who are not mad. By this, both the perception of duality and the experience of affliction are refuted. //25//
START MandUpK 4.26 Since there is no external cause, therefore— the mind does not touch an object, nor likewise an appearance of an object.
For since the object is unreal, the appearance of the object is not distinct from it.
The mind does not contact an external object as its objective support, nor does it [contact] the appearance of an object, because it is consciousness, like a dream-mind;
for even in the waking state, the external object such as sound and so forth is unreal, just like a dream-object, and because of the reasons already stated.
Nor is the appearance of objects separate from the mind; for it is the mind itself that appears as objects such as jars, just as in a dream. //26//
START MandUpK 4.27:
But then, if the jar and so forth do not exist, the mind’s appearance as a jar and so forth must be a misconception (*viparyāsa*).
And if that is the case, one must point out some instance where there is no misconception.
To this it is replied:
The mind does not always come into contact with a causal object throughout the three times.
How, then, can there be a misconception for one who is without a causal object? (MandUk 4.27)
The mind never touches the sign (nimitta), which is the object, even throughout the three times—past, future, and present.

For if it were to touch anything at all, that would be non-erroneous (aviparyāsa) and thus the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Therefore, in comparison to that, the appearance of a jar or the like when no jar exists would be an error; however, there is never any touching of an object by the mind.
Therefore, how could there be a distortion (viparyāsa) for that mind which is without a cause?
The intention is that in no way does distortion exist.
For this indeed is the very nature of the mind: that it appears as such [as a thing] even when a cause, such as a jar, does not exist. //27//

The statement of the Buddhist proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin), beginning with "The designation has a cause" and ending with these words, which aims at refuting the position of the proponent of external objects, was approved by the Teacher. Taking that very [argument] as the reason for refuting that position, this is now stated: START MandUpK 4.28: *prajñapteḥ sanimittatvam ityādyetadantaṃ vijñānavādino bauddhasya vacanaṃ bāhyārthavādipakṣapratiṣedhaparam ācāryeṇānumoditam / tadeva hetuṃ kṛtvā tatpakṣapratiṣedhāya tadidam ucyate-*
Therefore, the mind is not born, nor is that which is seen by the mind born;
those who perceive its birth truly perceive a footstep in the sky.

Since the Vijñānavādin accepts that the mind appears as a jar and so forth even when the jar and such do not exist, and we likewise approve of this because it accords with the vision of reality, it follows that the appearance of that mind as something arising must also be possible only while its actual birth does not exist; therefore, the mind is not born, just as the object seen by the mind is not born.
Therefore, those proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādins*) who perceive the birth of that mind, as well as its momentariness, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth—

perceiving that the nature of the mind cannot be seen by that very same mind— they are like those who see the tracks of birds in the sky. Thus, the meaning is that they are even more audacious than other dualists, since these proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*) also perceive [such things].

Those who thus profess the emptiness of all things, including even the emptiness of their own philosophical system, are even more reckless than that; they are like those who wish to grasp space with their fists. //28//
By the reasons stated above, it is established that Brahman is unborn and one; this verse is intended to conclude the result of that which was initially proposed as the thesis:
"Since the unborn is born from it, therefore non-birth is its nature."
No alteration of the primordial nature (prakṛti) will ever occur in any way whatsoever.
Those who maintain that the unborn mind is born as Brahman itself imagine that this unborn [mind] is born because its nature (prakṛti) is non-origination;
therefore, for that reason, no transformation—that is, birth—can ever occur from a nature whose form is unborn. //29//

Furthermore, this other defect is stated regarding those who maintain that the transmigratory existence and liberation of the self possess ultimate reality: "The finitude of a beginningless transmigratory existence cannot be established."
And for liberation that has a beginning, there could be no infinity.

The finitude—that is, the termination—of saṃsāra, which is beginningless and devoid of a past limit, will not be established; it will not attain proof through reasoning. For no entity whatsoever that is beginningless has been observed in the world to possess an end.
If it is argued that the continuity of the relationship between seed and sprout is intended to be unbroken, [we reply:]...
Likewise, infinity will not belong to liberation, which has a beginning arising at the time of the attainment of consciousness,
because it is not observed in things such as jars;
if it is argued that there is no fault because it is non-substantial, like the destruction of a jar or similar objects, [we reply:]...
Furthermore, there would be a loss of the thesis that liberation exists as an ultimate reality;
and precisely because it would be non-existent, like a hare's horn, it would lack even the quality of having a beginning. //30//
That which does not exist at the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present. Being similar to the unreal, they are perceived as if they were real. (MandUpK 4.31)
The purposiveness of those [dream objects] is contradicted within the dream itself;
therefore, because they possess a beginning and an end, they are indeed remembered as being purely false.
The two verses concerning unreality (*vaitathya*), which were previously explained, are recited here in connection with the consequence that there would be no liberation from *saṃsāra*. (31–32)
All phenomena are false in a dream, because they show the end of the body; when this region has ceased to exist, how indeed can there be a perception of beings?
The meaning of the statement, "The signlessness of the sign is intended through the vision of reality," is elaborated upon by these verses. //33//
It is not logical that [the soul] goes [to another world] for the sake of perception, because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of such a journey; moreover,
once awakened, no one at all is found in that place.

In the waking state, the time for going and coming and the location are fixed by measure; because of the absence of such restriction in dream, there is no traveling to another place—this is the meaning. //34//
Having deliberated with friends and others, one does not perceive [the dream] upon awakening; nor does one see anything whatsoever that was grasped [therein] once awakened. (MandUpK 4.35)
Having deliberated together with friends and others, one does not find that very counsel upon waking;
nor does one obtain whatever gold or other wealth was taken [in the dream].
For these reasons, people do not travel to another country in a dream. //35//
And in a dream, the body is unreal because it is seen as distinct from another;
as is the body, so too everything perceived by the mind is unreal.
The body that is seen in a dream is devoid of substantial reality (*avastuka*), because it is seen as distinct from another body designated as "one's own" during sleep.
Just as the body seen in a dream is non-existent, so too everything seen by the mind is devoid of substantial reality even in the waking state, because it is seen by the mind; this is the meaning.
Since it is equal to a dream, the waking state is also unreal—this is the sense of the section. //36//
Furthermore, the unreality of waking objects is established from this [verse]: "Because it is perceived like the waking state, the dream is held to have that [waking] as its cause."
But because it is the cause of that [waking state], that very [state] is considered the waking state.

Because the waking state is perceived in the very same manner as the waking state itself—in the form of subject and object—it is not a dream; that [waking state] is the cause of this dream, and that dream is held to be its effect, namely the waking state.
Since it has that as its cause and is the effect of that waking state, that waking state belongs only to the one who perceives the dream, and not to others.
This is the intended meaning, just as in the case of a dream.

Just as a dream, while being merely an object seen in a dream, appears as if it were a common, existing entity, so too—because it is caused by that [dream]—it appears as if it were a common, existing entity;
however, it is not a common, existing entity, but is just like a dream. This is the intended meaning. //37//
[Objection: Even if the waking object has the dream as its cause, it cannot be unreal like a dream;
for the dream is seen to be extremely fleeting, whereas the waking state is perceived as stable.
This may indeed be so for those who lack discernment;
however, for those with discernment, the arising of any entity whatsoever is not established.
Therefore, because arising is not established, everything is declared to be unborn.
And there is no way whatsoever for that which is non-existent to arise from that which is existent.

Because origination is not established, it is stated in the Vedānta texts that "the Self alone is everything, therefore everything is unborn," as in: "For he is unborn, both within and without" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
Even if you think that a dream arises from a waking state which is real, that is incorrect;
for in the world, there is no possibility of an unreal, non-existent thing arising from a real, existent one.
For the existence of non-existent things, such as a hare's horn and the like, is not observed in any way whatsoever. //38//
START MandUpK 4.39:

But was it not stated by you yourself that the dream state is the effect of the waking state? How then can it be said that its production is unestablished? Listen to how the relationship of cause and effect is intended by us in this regard:
Having seen what is unreal while awake, one sees it in a dream, being absorbed in that;
and having seen even the unreal in a dream, one does not see it upon waking.

Having seen in the waking state an unreal, non-existent object imagined as a snake in a rope, one who is permeated by its existence and absorbed in it perceives it even in a dream, conceptualizing it in the form of subject and object just as in the waking state.
Likewise, having seen such an unreal thing even in a dream, one does not see it upon waking, no longer conceptualizing it.
By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that similarly, having seen something in the waking state, one may at times not see it in a dream.
Therefore, the waking state is said to be the cause of the dream state, not because it is ultimately real. //39//
START MandUpK 4.40 But from the perspective of ultimate reality, the relationship of cause and effect is not tenable for anything in any manner whatsoever. How so?
That which is non-existent does not have a non-existent cause; likewise, that which is existent-and-non-existent does not have such a cause.
That which exists does not have a real cause; how could that which does not exist have a real cause?

There is no non-existent thing that has a non-existent cause; that is, there is no non-existent thing such as a rabbit’s horn for which a non-existent thing such as its own flower serves as the cause or reason.
Likewise, even an existent entity such as a jar does not have a non-existent thing such as a rabbit’s horn as its effect.
Similarly, an existent thing such as a jar does not have another existent thing such as a jar as its effect.
How could an effect that is non-existent (asat) possibly arise from [a cause]? Nor is any other relationship between cause and effect possible or even conceivable.
Therefore, the intention is that for those who possess discernment, the relationship of cause and effect is simply unestablished for anyone. //40//
START MandUpK 4.41 Again, dispelling the suspicion that there might be a causal relationship even between the waking and dreaming states— both of which are non-existent— he says:
"Just as through delusion one might perceive unthinkable things in the waking state as if they were real,"
Likewise, due to cognitive distortion, one perceives phenomena within that very dream.

The meaning is as follows: just as someone in the waking state, due to error (*viparyāsa*) and lack of discernment (*aviveka*), might conceptualize unthinkable things—such as a rope-snake—which ought not to be thought of, as if they were real and as if he were actually touching them; in that same way, in a dream, one conceptualizes objects such as elephants as if seeing them due to error.
One sees them only there [in the dream], and not as things arising from the waking state. //41//
Because of perception and because of conventional practice, for those who maintain that things possess substantial reality,
the Buddhas have taught "origination" (jāti) as a teaching for those who are always terrified of "non-origination" (ajāti).
Furthermore, even that "birth" which was taught and pointed out by the Buddhas who propound non-duality—
the meaning being "from apprehension," that is, from perception—
and "from conventional practice," that is, from the performance of duties such as those pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*).

For those who assert that things exist as real entities— those who habitually say "there is a real entity," who possess firm attachment, who have faith, and whose discernment is dull— that birth was taught by those two reasons as a means to an undesirable end;
let them, for now, accept it.
However, for those who practice Vedānta, discrimination regarding the non-born, non-dual Self will arise spontaneously, and not through the intellect of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-buddhi*).

For those Vedic scholars, due to their gross intellect, always tremble at the "non-born"—that is, the reality of non-origination—thinking it to be the destruction of the self; thus they are undiscriminating.
It was said that this [teaching] is a means for their introduction [to the truth]. //42//
For those who tremble at the unborn [Brahman] because they perceive it as something distinct, their fears will vanish;
the defects arising from the notion of birth will not prevail, and even if a defect remains, it will be slight.

The meaning is that those who, out of apprehension regarding non-arising and the reality of non-arising, depart from the non-dual Self— which is "existence" because of such perception and conduct— and go toward what is contrary, falling into duality;

for those who fear non-arising yet possess faith and rely upon the true path, the defects of birth— the defects caused by the perception of birth— will not succeed, they will not reach fulfillment, because they have set out upon the path of discernment.
Even if some fault should occur, it will be very slight; the meaning is that it will be caused solely by the failure to attain right vision. //43//
[Objection: But surely duality as a real entity exists, because perception and common practice are authoritative means of knowledge.
[Reply: No; for perception and common practice are subject to deviation.
How is there a deviation? It is said:

Just as a "magical elephant" is spoken of because of its perception and its functional behavior, so too a real entity is said to exist because of its perception and its functional behavior. (MandUpK 4.44)

For an illusory elephant (*māyāhastī*) is indeed perceived as if it were a real elephant; people behave toward it as they would toward an elephant, and it is called an "elephant" because of its connection with properties associated with elephants, such as being bound or mounted—even though it does not exist. Just so, because of such perception and conventional behavior, it is said that there exists a dualistic reality in the form of difference.
Therefore, the intention is that perception and conventional behavior do not serve as proofs for the actual existence of a dualistic reality. //44//

Furthermore, he says that the ultimate reality is that true entity which serves as the basis for the false cognitions of genus and so forth: "It appears as a genus, as movement, and likewise as a substance."
Unborn, immovable, devoid of substantiality, consciousness is peaceful and non-dual.
That which appears as if it were born, though it is unborn, is called "appearance as birth," such as when one says, "Devadatta is born.
That which appears as if it were moving, though it is not moving, is called "appearance as movement."
Just as one says, "that very Devadatta goes.

An appearance of an object (*vastvābhāsa*) refers to an object (*vastu*), a substance (*dravya*), or a substratum (*dharmin*) that appears in such a way; thus it is called an "appearance of an object.
For example, just as that very Devadatta is perceived as "fair-skinned" or "tall," Devadatta appears in this manner: he moves, he is tall, he is fair-skinned, and so forth.
In ultimate reality, however, you are unmoving, non-substantial, and without material constituents; what is it that is of such a nature?
It is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is representation-only (*vijñapti*);
it is quiescent because it is devoid of birth and other such characteristics.
Therefore, it is non-dual; such is the meaning. //45//
In this way the mind is not born; in this way all phenomena are known to be unborn.
Those who understand it thus do not fall into error.

Thus, for the reasons stated above, the mind is not born; likewise, all phenomena (*dharma*) are remembered by the knowers of Brahman as unborn (*aja*). The plural form "phenomena" is used figuratively because the non-dual reality conforms to the distinctions of various bodies.

In this very way, those who understand the non-dual reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*)—which is consciousness as described, devoid of birth and other such attributes—and who have abandoned external desires, do not fall again into the ocean of the darkness of ignorance and its errors.
“Then what delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Iśa Upaniṣad 7)—from such scriptural verses as these. //46//
Beginning with Mandūkakārikā 4.47,
intending to elaborate upon the aforementioned vision of ultimate reality, he says:
"Just as the whirling of a firebrand appears as straight, curved, and so forth..."
Likewise, the vibration of consciousness appears as the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.

For just as in the world the flickering of a firebrand—the movement of a torch—appears in various forms such as straight or curved, so too does the vibration of consciousness appear as the apprehended and the apprehender, meaning it appears as the subject and the object.
What is this vibration of consciousness? It is called "vibration" only in a figurative sense, for it is [mere appearance] through ignorance (*avidyā*).
For there is no movement of this consciousness;
indeed, it has been stated that it is "unborn and immovable. //47//
Just as a firebrand that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging,
so too consciousness that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging.
Just as that very firebrand, when not flickering—that is, devoid of vibration—is unborn, unmanifest, and undecaying in its straight or other forms;

so too, that which was flickering due to ignorance becomes, upon the cessation of ignorance, non-flickering, unmanifest, unborn, immovable, and free from the forms of birth and so forth—this is the meaning. //48//
Furthermore:
"When a firebrand is whirled, the appearances do not arise from anywhere else."
They do not enter the firebrand from anywhere other than that motionless state.

In that very same firebrand, while it is flickering, the appearances of straightness, curvature, and so forth do not arise from the firebrand itself; they do not come from some other source and thus do not originate elsewhere.
Nor do they issue out from that motionless firebrand to another place, nor do they enter back into that very same motionless firebrand. //49//
Furthermore:
Nor have they emerged from the firebrand, because of their lack of connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*).
The same would apply to consciousness as well, because there is no difference in the appearance.

The appearances do not emerge from the firebrand, because they lack the connection with substantiality (dravyatva), just like houses and so forth. "Substantiality" (dravyatva) means the state of being a substance; the absence of that is the "absence of substantiality.
The meaning is that, due to the connection with the absence of substantiality—that is, by virtue of being devoid of substantiality—there is an absence of the nature of a real entity (vastutva).
For entry and so forth are possible for a real entity (vastu), not for a non-entity (avastu).
Likewise, even cognitions would possess the appearances of genus and so forth, because there is no distinction in the appearance itself; they are identical. //50//
To explain how there is equality, he says:
"When consciousness itself is vibrating, the appearances do not originate from elsewhere."
They do not enter into consciousness, which is motionless and nothing other than that.
They do not emerge from consciousness, because they lack substantiality;
since they are always inconceivable, they possess neither the nature of cause nor effect.
Everything regarding consciousness is equal to a whirling firebrand;
however, the constant motion of consciousness is its distinguishing feature.
To the question, "If consciousness is motionless, by what are the appearances of birth and so forth produced? he says:
Because they lack the nature of cause and effect, because the relationship of produced and producer is untenable, and because they are of the nature of non-existence, they are always inconceivable.

Just as the cognition of straightness and so forth is seen to occur toward a mere fire-brand despite the absence of actual straightness and the like, so too, in the case of birth and so forth, the cognition of birth and the like within mere consciousness is purely false; such is the collective meaning. //51-52//
START MandUpK 4.53 Even for those who maintain that the reality of the Self is the one unborn [principle], yet postulate a relationship of cause and effect therein,
it must follow that one substance would be the cause of another substance, and indeed, one thing would be distinct from another.
Neither substantiality nor the existence of other things is possible for dharmas.
One substance may be the cause or the reason for another distinct substance, but it cannot be the cause of itself.
Furthermore, in the world, no non-substance is observed to be an independent cause of anything.

Moreover, the state of being a substance (dravyatva) is not applicable to phenomena or to selves, nor is their distinctness from anything else established, such that they could attain the status of being either a cause or an effect of something else.
Therefore, because it is neither a substance nor distinct [from itself], the meaning is that the Self is neither the effect nor the cause of anything. //53//
Thus, phenomena are not born from the mind, nor is the mind born from phenomena; in this way,
the wise enter into the non-arising of cause and effect.

Thus, for the reasons stated above, the mind is nothing other than the very nature of self-cognition; therefore, external phenomena are not born from the mind, nor is the mind born from external phenomena.

Since all phenomena are merely manifestations of the nature of cognition itself, in this way, neither does a fruit arise from a cause, nor does a cause arise from a fruit. Entering into and resolving upon this non-arising of cause and fruit, they realize the absolute absence of both cause and fruit within the self.
The meaning is "one who knows Brahman. //54//

Furthermore, regarding those who are attached to cause and effect, it is said: "What would happen for them?"—namely, [the thought]: "I am the agent of the cause called merit and demerit; my merit and demerit exist; their fruit shall be experienced by me at some other time, having been born within some class of living beings."
As long as there is the entry into cause and effect, so long does the arising of cause and effect continue;
when the entry into cause and effect has ceased, there is no further arising of cause and effect.
As long as there is an obsession with cause and effect—the non-apprehension of cause and effect and the superimposition of a self—that is what is meant by "being possessed by that mind.
During that time, there is the emergence of cause and effect, and the continuous operation of merit and demerit along with their results.

However, when the obsession with cause and effect produced by ignorance is removed by the realization of non-duality as described—just as possession by a spirit is removed by the power of mantras and medicines—then, once that [obsession] has perished, there is no further emergence of cause and effect.
START MandUpK 4.56 If there is the arising of cause and effect, then what is the fault? It is said:
As long as there is the immersion in cause and effect, so long is saṃsāra extended.
When the penetration of cause and effect has ceased, one does not enter into saṃsāra.
The meaning is that as long as the penetration of cause and effect is not reversed by right vision (samyagdarśana), saṃsāra remains extensive and long-lasting;
however, once the penetration of cause and effect is exhausted, one does not enter into saṃsāra again due to the absence of its cause. //56//

START MandUpK 4.57 But surely, since there exists nothing other than the unborn Self, how is it that you speak of the arising and destruction of cause and effect, as well as of transmigratory existence?
Listen—
Everything arises through conventional reality; therefore, there is indeed no eternalism.
For everything is unborn in its true being; therefore, there is indeed no nihilism.
Convention (*saṃvṛti*) is concealment; it is the sphere of ignorance, worldly discourse. Through that convention, everything arises.
Therefore, within the sphere of ignorance, there is indeed no eternal or permanent [reality].
Hence, saṃsāra, characterized by arising and destruction, is said to be extended.

However, because everything is unborn and is indeed the Self by virtue of its existence as the ultimate reality (paramārthasadbhāva), there is no destruction of anything whatsoever—such as cause and effect—due to the absence of birth; this is the meaning. //57//
Those phenomena which are said to be born are not born in reality;
their birth is like an illusion, and that illusion does not exist.

Those selves and other phenomena which are conceptualized as "arising"—such as those described above—are designated by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, phenomena arise only conventionally;
they do not arise in reality or in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, that arising of those aforementioned phenomena by way of convention should be understood as being like an illusion, just as an illusion arises.
Is it then a real entity called "illusion"?
Not so; that illusion does not exist.
The intended meaning is that "illusion" is a designation for that which is non-existent. //58//
START MandUpK 4.59 To explain how the birth of those phenomena is like an illusion, it says:
Just as from a seed consisting of illusion, a sprout consisting of that same illusion is born;
It is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation; such is the application of this principle to all phenomena.

Just as from a seed consisting of illusion (māyā) there arises a sprout consisting of illusion—neither a non-sprout, nor eternal, nor subject to annihilation or destruction because it is unreal—in the same way, the application of birth, destruction, and so forth to phenomena (dharmas) is logical; however, in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ), neither the birth nor the destruction of phenomena is tenable. This is the meaning. //59//
Among all dharmas that are beyond destruction, there is no designation of "eternal" or "non-eternal";
where the [distinctions of] castes do not exist, there "discrimination" is not spoken of.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, regarding those things which are self-natured, eternally of one taste, and whose existence is mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra-sattāka*), neither the designation "eternal" nor "non-eternal" operates; this is the meaning.
Wherein and in which things these [qualities] are described, those syllables (*varṇa*)—which are sounds (*śabda*)—do not operate to designate or to manifest them; this is the meaning.
Distinction (*viveka*) is the state of being distinct (*viviktatā*), such as "this is thus"; therein, it is not said to be "eternal" or "non-eternal."
This is because of the Vedic scripture (śruti): "From which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1). //60//
Just as in a dream the mind moves through illusion appearing as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind moves through illusion appearing as a duality. (MandUpK 4.61)
The mind, though non-dual, appears as dual in a dream—of this there is no doubt;
likewise, it is non-dual yet appears as dual in the waking state—of this there is no doubt.

Furthermore, that which is the domain of speech regarding the non-dual state of mere consciousness from the perspective of ultimate reality is merely the vibration of the mind, not [the object] itself in ultimate reality.
These two verses express this meaning. (61–62)
Furthermore, for this reason, duality is beyond the range of speech:
"The dreamer, moving about in a dream, [sees] those situated in the ten directions."
He always perceives those living beings who are born from eggs or born from sweat.

"One who sees dreams" (*svapnadṛk*) is one who, while moving about—that is, wandering—in a dream, within the state of dreaming, constantly beholds living beings, creatures existing in the ten directions, whether born from eggs or born from sweat. If this is so, what follows? It is said:
Those objects perceived by the mind of the dreamer do not exist apart from it;
likewise, this very object of perception is held to be the mind of the dreamer itself.

The mind of the dreamer is "svapnadṛkcitta"; those living beings (jīvas) are seen by that [mind], and therefore they do not exist as something separate from that dreamer's mind—the meaning is that they do not exist.
For it is the mind itself that is conceptualized in the form of various distinctions such as multiple living beings.
Likewise, this very mind of the dreamer is itself an object of perception for that [dreamer].
Therefore, that which is seen by the dreamer is what is seen;
thus, the meaning is that apart from the dreamer, there is no such thing as a mind. //64//
While awake in the waking state, one always perceives those living beings— whether born from eggs or born from sweat— who reside within the ten directions. (MandUpK 4.65)
Those objects are not found to exist separately from the waking consciousness that perceives them;
likewise, this very visible world is held to be the mind of the waking person.

Living beings perceived by one who is awake are not distinct from his mind, because they are objects of observation for that mind, like the living beings observed by the mind of a dreamer. And that mind, which consists of the observation of living beings, is not distinct from the observer, because it is an object of observation for the observer, like the dreaming mind. The rest has already been explained. (65–66)
For both of these are mutually perceived; yet it is asked, "What is that which exists?
In that view, neither of the two is grasped, as both are devoid of defining characteristics.
The living being and the mind— both the mind and its objects— are mutually visible and mutually accessible;
for that which is called "mind" exists in dependence upon objects such as the living being,
and the visible [object], such as the living being, exists in dependence upon the mind.
Therefore, those two are seen as distinct from one another;

hence it is said that "nothing exists," whether it be the mind (*citta*) or that which is perceived by the mind (*cittekṣaṇīya*). This is what is stated by the discerning (*vivekin*): "Does that [object] exist? For just as in a dream neither an elephant nor the thought of an elephant exists, so too is it for the discerning in this case—this is the intended meaning.

How so? That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇā*), meaning a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which is devoid of such a characteristic is the "characterized" (*lakṣya*). Both the mind (*citta*) and mental objects (*caitya*)—this duality—is grasped precisely through that [mental] conception and as that very mind.
For a jar is not grasped by setting aside the cognition of the jar, nor is the cognition of the jar grasped by setting aside the jar.
The intention is that, in this regard, a distinction between the means of cognition and the object of cognition cannot be conceived. //67//
Just as the living being consisting of a dream is born and also dies, so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist. (MandUpK 4.68)
Just as a living being consisting of illusion is born and also dies,
so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist.
Just as a magically created being is born and also dies,
so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist.

That which is made of illusion by a magician, or that which is produced as a magical creation through mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth; just as beings born from eggs arise and die within dreams, illusions, and magical creations, so too those characterized as humans and the like are non-existent, being merely the conceptual constructions of the mind—this is the meaning. (Verses 68–70)
No living being is ever born; its origin does not exist. This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born. (MandUkK 4.71)
Regarding the domain of conventional truth (*vyavahārasatya*), it has been stated that for living beings (*jīva*), birth, death, and so forth are like those of a person in a dream;
however, the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is that no living being is ever born. The rest is as previously explained. //71//
This duality, appearing as the grasped and the grasper, is merely the vibration of the mind; therefore,
the mind is proclaimed to be eternally objectless and unattached.

The duality of the grasped and the grasper is entirely just the vibration of the mind; from the perspective of ultimate reality, the mind is itself the Self. Therefore, it is proclaimed to be eternally unattached because it is objectless.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "For this person is indeed unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15–16).
For attachment occurs only toward an object for one who possesses an object.
The meaning is that because it is without an object, the mind is unattached. //72//
START MandUpK 4.73:

Now, if it is argued that the mind’s lack of attachment (*asaṅgatva*) does not constitute non-attachment (*niḥsaṅgatā*) because objects such as the teacher, the scripture, and the disciple still exist, this is not a fault. Why?
That which exists by way of imagined convention does not exist in the ultimate sense;
that which exists by way of dependent convention may exist, but it does not exist from the perspective of the ultimate.
Whatever entity, such as the scriptures and so forth, exists, that exists by way of imagined convention (*kalpitasaṃvṛti*);

and because it is imagined as a means for attaining the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is a convention. That which exists by way of such [convention] does not exist in the ultimate sense; it is not found.
It has been stated that when [reality] is known, duality does not exist.

Furthermore, whatever category of object might exist through the conventional reality of dependence (*paratantra-saṃvṛti*) or by way of the linguistic usage of other treatises, that does not exist at all when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, it is rightly said: "By that, he is celebrated as being unattached. (73)
START MandUpK 4.74:
But if the scriptures and so forth are conventional, would this conceptualization that "he is unborn" also be conventional?
True, it would be so.
The unborn is so by way of imagined convention; in the ultimate sense, it is not even unborn.
However, through the establishment of the dependent nature and the rest, it is born by way of convention.

The term "unborn" (aja) is spoken of only through the conventional reality (saṃvṛti) imagined by one's own or other scriptures. In the ultimate sense (paramārtha), even the unborn does not exist; for that which is called "unborn" with respect to the establishment of another school's doctrine—by way of the dependent nature (paratantra)—is actually born conventionally.
Therefore, the meaning is that this conceptualization of being "unborn" does not apply at all to the domain of the ultimate truth. //74//
START MandUpK 4.75 Since it has unreal objects, therefore: There is adherence to the non-existent; duality does not exist therein.
Having realized the non-existence of duality, he becomes signless and is not born again.
There is merely an adherence to a duality that is unreal;
"adherence" means nothing more than grasping.
Duality does not exist therein.
Since the cause of birth is merely false attachment, therefore, having realized the non-existence of duality, one who is signless and whose false attachment to duality has ceased is not born. //75//
When one does not find causes— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
then the mind is not born; in the absence of a cause, how can there be a fruit?

Dharmas prescribed for specific castes and stages of life (*āśrama*), when performed without being devoid of blessings (*āśis*), are the supreme and exclusive dharmas that cause the attainment of godhood and other such states.

Those mixed with unrighteousness (*adharma*) which result in the attainment of human status and so forth are middling. And those particular activities characterized by unrighteousness which cause the attainment of animal births and so forth are inferior.

Knowing that the self-nature (*ātmatattva*)— which is one alone, without a second, devoid of all conceptual constructions, and distinct from those [states] imagined as superior, middling, and inferior through ignorance— one neither acquires nor perceives them. Just as a discerning person does not see the impurity seen by fools in the sky,
so too at that time the mind is neither born nor produced in the forms of gods and so forth, or in the form of superior, middling, and inferior fruits.
For indeed, when a cause is absent, an effect does not arise, just as crops and the like do not arise in the absence of seeds and so forth. //76//
It has been stated that "in the absence of causes, the mind does not arise.
Now, it is explained what kind of non-arising this non-arising of the mind is:
The non-arising of the signless mind is equanimous non-duality,
because all that is seen by the mind is indeed unborn.

The non-arising known as liberation— which belongs to the mind that is signless because the causes of arising called dharma and adharma have been discarded by the vision of ultimate reality— is at all times and in all states equal, undifferentiated, and non-dual;
the meaning is that even previously, this entire non-dual mind was simply unborn and unarisen.

Since that which is perceived by the mind prior to consciousness is non-dual, and since birth is likewise [non-dual], therefore the non-arising of the entire mind—which is unborn—is always and everywhere non-dual; it does not sometimes exist and sometimes not exist. The meaning is that it is always of a single nature. //77//
START MandUpK 4.78 By the reasoning already stated, because of the absence of the two causes that give rise to birth:
Having understood that the causal condition is real, and not obtaining any separate cause;
One attains that state which is free from sorrow, free from desire, and fearless.

Having realized the state of signlessness (*animittatā*), which is the truth in its ultimate sense (*paramārtharūpa*), and no longer obtaining—meaning not grasping—the various causes such as ritual acts (*dharma*) for the sake of attaining births as gods and so forth, he, having abandoned external longings, attains the fearless state that is free from desire, grief, and the like, and devoid of ignorance (*avidyā*) and other afflictions; the meaning is that he is not born again. //78//
For it is due to the persistent clinging to what is unreal that [the mind] proceeds toward that which appears similar;
once it has realized the non-existence of the object, it turns away from it without attachment. (MandUpK 4.79)

Because there is an adherence to what is unreal, there is the determination of the existence of duality where duality does not exist; this is adherence to the unreal. Therefore, due to that form of delusion consisting of ignorance, the mind proceeds toward that which is similar and conforms to it.
When one has realized the non-existence of that dual entity, then, being unattached and indifferent, the mind completely turns away from the object of that adherence to the unreal. (79)
For the state of one who has desisted from activity and does not engage in it is indeed motionless;
that is the object of the Buddhas—namely, that sameness which is unborn and non-dual. (MandUpK 4.80)

For one who has desisted from the object of duality and does not engage with any other object, there occurs through the vision of non-existence a state of the mind that is motionless, devoid of movement, and identical to the very nature of Brahman.

This state of the mind, which is of the nature of Brahman and characterized by being a single, dense mass of non-dual consciousness, is indeed the sphere of experience for the Buddhas who perceive ultimate reality; therefore, it is the supreme similarity—undifferentiated, unborn, and non-dual. //80//
START MandUpK 4.81 Furthermore, he explains what kind of object this is for the Buddhas:
"It is unborn, sleepless, dreamless, and becomes self-luminous."
For this [Self] is indeed once-for-all manifest by virtue of its nature as the dharma-dhātu.
That dawn occurs by itself, not depending on the sun and so forth;
the meaning is that its nature is self-luminous.

"Shining once, it is always shining"—this means that this very reality called the Self (ātman), characterized in this way, exists by its own nature as a fundamental element (dhātu) and by its own nature as a real entity (vastu). //81//
START MandUpK 4.82:
Even though the ultimate reality is being explained in this way, why is it not grasped by worldly people? It is said:
"Happiness is constantly concealed, while suffering is perpetually revealed."
By the grasping of whichever phenomenon it may be, that Blessed One [is perceived].

Because, by grasping at—meaning by the obsession with grasping at—any dualistic entity or phenomenon through false adherence, happiness (*sukha*) is obscured, which means it is concealed without effort;
for in that case, the obscuration consists in the perception of duality, and no further exertion is required. And suffering (*duḥkha*) is unveiled, meaning it is made manifest.

Because knowledge of the ultimate truth is difficult to attain, the meaning is that this Blessed One is the God who is non-dual with the Self; therefore, the meaning is that even though he is spoken of many times by the Vedāntas and by the teachers, he cannot be known at all.
“Wondrous is the speaker; skilled is its obtainer,” according to the Śruti (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.7). //82//

START MandUpK 4.83 Even the subtle conceptual graspings of the learned, such as "it exists" or "it does not exist," are indeed veils over the Blessed Supreme Self; how much more so are those characterized by the intellect of foolish people? Demonstrating this point, he says:
"It exists, it does not exist, it both exists and does not exist, or again, it neither exists nor does not exist."
The fool indeed obscures [reality] with the notions of movement, stability, both, or neither.
A certain proponent of the self maintains that "the self exists";

another, a nihilist (*vaināśika*), maintains that "it does not exist"; another, a semi-nihilist (*ardhavaināśika*), maintains both "it exists" and "it does not exist," being a proponent of both being and non-being, such as the naked ascetic (*digvāsas*); and yet another, an absolute nihilist, maintains that "it does not exist, it does not exist."
In that regard, the state of existence is mobile because it is distinct from the impermanent things such as jars;
the state of non-existence is stable because it is always without distinction.
Both [the existent and the non-existent] are subject to movement and stability; thus, "existence" refers to being present, while "non-existence" refers to absolute non-being.

By means of these four modes—the moving, the stable, both, and the absence of both—every fool who lacks discernment, such as those who propound existence, non-existence, and so forth, indeed obscures the Blessed One.

Although a learned man is in fact a fool because he does not understand the reality of ultimate truth, what need is there to mention the person who is deluded regarding intrinsic nature? This is the intended meaning. //83//
Furthermore, what is the nature of the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) through the realization of which one becomes a wise man rather than a fool? To this he says:
"These four corners, however, are always occupied by the planets."
He by whom the Blessed One is seen as untouched by these [attributes] is all-seeing.

The "extremes" (*koṭyaḥ*) are said to be the conclusions reached by the treatises of various teachers, beginning with "it exists" and "it does not exist"—four such extremes. One who is always and at all times "obstructed" or covered by the "seizures" of these extremes—that is, by their grasping and conceptual determinations—is untouched even by those four extremes of "existence," "non-existence," and so forth, which belong to those very teachers; he is the Blessed One, free from the conceptual constructions of existence and the rest.

This refers to that sage by whom the person described in the Vedāntas and the Upaniṣads has been seen and known; he is all-seeing, omniscient, and a knower of the ultimate truth—this is the meaning. //84//
Having attained complete omniscience, the state of Brahminhood which is non-dual and devoid of beginning,
middle, or end— what more could one possibly strive for beyond this?

Having attained this aforementioned, entire, and complete omniscience—the state of Brahminhood—according to the Śruti: "He is a Brāhmaṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10) and "This is the eternal glory of the Brāhmaṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23); that non-dual state whose beginning, middle, and end—that is, its origination, maintenance, and dissolution—are not undergone, nor are they found, is the state of Brahminhood, which has no beginning, middle, or end.
Having attained and gained that very [Self], what more than this—beyond this attainment of the Self—does one strive for or exert oneself? The meaning is that there is no further purpose.
This is in accordance with such traditional texts (smṛti) as: "There is no purpose whatsoever for him by means of action" (Gītā 3.18). //85//
For this discipline (vinaya) of the wise is said to be tranquility (śama) in its natural state;
self-restraint (dama) arises from being naturally restrained. Thus, the man of knowledge should attain tranquility.
The discipline (*vinaya*) of the wise—that is, of the *brāhmaṇas*—is their state of being disciplined, which is their abiding in their own essential nature.
This very discipline is also tranquility (*śama*); it is called natural, inherent, and uncreated.
It is also self-restraint (*dama*), because Brahman is by its very nature restrained and because its form is inherently peaceful.

Thus, the knower of Brahman, which is inherently quiescent as previously described, shall go to—that is, abide in the nature of—Brahman, which is peace and inherent tranquility; this is the meaning. //86//

START MandUpK 4.87 Thus, because they are mutually contradictory and serve as the basis for the defects of passion and hatred— the causes of saṃsāra— the philosophical systems of the various teachers are false views. Having demonstrated this through their own internal logic, [the author] concludes that the non-dual vision alone— which is free from the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) and is not a locus for defects such as grasping— is the right view, being by nature quiescent.
Now begins the exposition of its own system:
That which possesses both an object and a perceiving subject is held to be worldly;
that which lacks an object but possesses a perceiving subject is held to be pure worldly. (MandUpK 4.87)
"Accompanied by an object" (*savastu*) means that which exists together with an object (*vastu*) that is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*);

likewise, "accompanied by apprehension" (*sopalambha*) means that which exists together with apprehension (*upalambha*). This dual nature, characterized by the grasped and the grasper, which is the basis for all worldly conventions such as treatises and so forth, is "worldly" (*laukika*)—that is, not departed from the world—and refers to the waking state.
Such is the definition of the waking state as intended in the Vedāntas:
it is devoid of reality because even conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is absent;

and it is "with apprehension" (*sopalambha*), meaning that there is an apprehension of things as if they were real entities, even though no such entity exists, and it functions together with that [apprehension].
The meaning is that "dream" (svapna) is intended as that which is pure, absolute, and distinct from the gross, worldly waking state, because it is not common to all living beings. //87//

That which is non-existent and non-perception is remembered as supramundane; this is always proclaimed by the Buddhas as knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is to be known. (MandUpK 4.88)
The non-perception of non-existent things and being devoid of the grasping of an object—this is the supramundane, for this very reason it transcends the world.
For the world has as its domain the grasping of objects; because that is absent, this state is remembered as "deep sleep," which is the seed of all activity.
