That knowledge by which the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*)— along with its means (*sopāya*), as well as the mundane (*laukika*), the purified mundane (*śuddhalaukika*), and the supramundane (*lokottara*)— is known in succession is "knowledge.
The objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are precisely these three,
because no object of knowledge can logically exist apart from them, and because all things imagined by various teachers (*prāvāduka*) are included within this very [classification].
The meaning is that the reality of the Self—non-dual and unborn, known as the Fourth (turya)—is to be understood as the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
This has been proclaimed at all times by the Buddhas, the knowers of Brahman who perceive the ultimate reality, as extending from the worldly level up to the limit of all that can be known. //88//

And when the threefold knowledge and that which is to be known have been understood by oneself in due order, omniscience indeed arises everywhere for the one of great intelligence in this world. (MandUpK 4.89)
And regarding knowledge— having as its objects the mundane and so forth— and the object of knowledge— the threefold mundane and so forth: first is the coarse mundane [knowledge],
and subsequently, through the absence of that, is the pure mundane [knowledge].

Thus, by the absence of the three states in succession— namely, through the state of being "thus" (tathābhāva) as supramundane (lokottara)— when the fourth state is known, which is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), non-dual, unborn, and fearless, then for one of great intellect (mahādhi), that very nature of the Self itself becomes omniscience (sarvajñatā); for he is "all" and he is "knowing," thus he is the "all-knower" (sarvajña), and his state is omniscience, which comes to pass here in this world.
The meaning is that for one who possesses such knowledge—because his intellect has as its object a reality that transcends all the world—this [knowledge] exists everywhere and at all times;

for once the true nature (svarūpa) has been known, there is no possibility of deviation. Indeed, for those who know the ultimate truth, there is no arising or suppression of knowledge, unlike other teachers (prāvāduka). //89//

Since worldly things and so forth have been taught in sequence as objects to be known, [the author] says the following so that there may be no suspicion of their ultimate reality: "Those things to be abandoned, those to be known, those to be attained, and those to be matured are to be understood according to their excellence."
The perception of these [three] is traditionally held to occur in three ways, except for that which is to be known [by direct realization].

The meaning is that the three states—the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—which are to be abandoned, such as the worldly state and so forth, must be removed from the Self like a snake from a rope by recognizing their non-existence therein.
That which is to be known here is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), free from the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭivarjita*).
To be attained are the means called scholarship, childlike innocence, and silence, by a mendicant who has renounced the three external desires.
The faults such as passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth, which are called "astringents" (kaṣāya), are to be cooked— that is, they are to be eliminated.
The meaning is that all these things— those to be abandoned, those to be known, those to be attained, and those to be cooked— are to be understood by the monk as means,
starting from the very beginning, from the foremost path.

Regarding those [categories] beginning with what is to be abandoned (*heya*), apart from the single Brahman which is to be known as the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), their "apprehension" (*upalambha*)—that is, perception—is merely a conceptual construction of ignorance (*avidyā*). The meaning is that among these three—the object to be abandoned, the means of abandonment, and the goal to be attained—they are recognized by the knowers of Brahman as being devoid of ultimate reality. //90//
START MandUpK 4.91 But from the perspective of ultimate reality— like space by nature, all phenomena are to be known as beginningless.
Indeed, no diversity whatsoever exists among them anywhere.

By their very nature and essence, all *dharmas*—the selves (*ātman*) to be known by those seeking liberation—are like space, equal to space, being subtle, stainless, and all-pervading; they are beginningless and eternal.
Anticipating the doubt that the use of the plural number might imply actual diversity, he says: "In any place, there does not exist even a particle's worth of multiplicity among them. (91)
Even the knowability of phenomena exists only conventionally and not in the ultimate sense; thus he says:
"All phenomena are by their very nature primordially awakened and perfectly certain."
He who possesses such patience is fit for immortality.

Because the Buddhas are primordial Buddhas by their very nature—that is, by their inherent essence—just as the sun is by its very nature eternally luminous, so too they are eternally awakened; this is the meaning. All phenomena (dharmas) and all selves (ātmanas) are thus.
Furthermore, no determination needs to be made regarding them, for their essential nature is eternally determined; this is the meaning.

It is not of a nature that is subject to doubt as to whether it is "thus" or "not thus. For the seeker of liberation who, in the manner described, is always indifferent to the certainty of cognition— whether for his own sake or for the sake of others—
just as the sun is eternally independent of any other light for its own sake and for the sake of others, so it becomes.

Patience is the state of being indifferent toward the duty of awakening; it always conduces to one's own immortality—that is, to the state of nectar—and becomes capable of liberation; this is the meaning. //92//
Likewise, he states that there is no need for the performance of pacification regarding the self:
"For [all things] are primordially peaceful, unarisen, and by their very nature perfectly extinguished."
All phenomena are equal and undifferentiated; they are unborn, equanimous, and fearless.

Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are primordially quiescent, eternally peaceful, unarisen, and unborn by their very nature—meaning they are perfectly extinguished and their intrinsic nature is thoroughly stilled—and because they are equal and undifferentiated, being both equal and non-distinct;
and because the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) is unborn, equanimous, fearless, and pure, therefore there is no peace or liberation to be accomplished. This is the meaning.
For nothing whatsoever produced could be purposeful for that which possesses a single, eternal nature. //93//
START MandUpK 4.94:
Those who have realized the aforementioned supreme reality are alone the non-miserable in this world; all others are indeed miserable. Thus he says:
"But there is truly no fearlessness for those who always move within the realm of duality."
Those who speak of distinctions are inclined toward duality; therefore, they are considered wretched.
Because they are inclined toward difference and follow after difference—meaning they follow the cycle of transmigration—who are they?
Those who speak of things as separate, that is, those whose speech is "separate" (pṛthagvādāḥ), meaning dualists;
therefore, they are considered wretched and base.
The meaning is that because there is no fearlessness or purity for those who move about in their divisions, remaining always on the dualistic path imagined by ignorance;
therefore, it is entirely appropriate that they possess wretchedness—this is the intended sense. //94//

Regarding this reality of the supreme truth (*paramārthatattva*), which cannot be fathomed by those who are not great-souled, who are unlearned, who stand outside the Vedānta, who are petty, and of limited intelligence— the text says:
"But those few who shall become firmly resolved regarding the unborn and the equal..."
For they indeed possess great wisdom in the world, yet the world does not fathom that [wisdom].

If even those such as the Sāṅkhyas and others should become perfectly certain that "in this very way, equality is the ultimate reality," they alone would be the possessors of great knowledge in the world— those whose knowledge has for its object the unsurpassed reality—
and that path, the ultimate reality known by them, is not entered, descended into, nor made an object of experience by any other person of ordinary intellect.
[This is said] of one who has become the self of all beings and who seeks the welfare of all beings.
"Even the gods are bewildered on the path as they seek the footprints of the trackless one;
'Just as the movement of birds in the sky cannot be perceived' (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 239.23, 24)," according to such traditional teachings. //95//
START MandUpK 4.96 To explain how there is "great knowledge," he says:
Knowledge is held to be unborn and non-transferred among unborn phenomena.
Because knowledge does not proceed [into it], it is therefore proclaimed to be "unattached" (asaṅga).

In unborn, unarisen, and immovable phenomena, self-nature and immovable knowledge are held to exist, just as heat and light exist in the sun. Therefore, knowledge is held to be unborn because it does not transfer to another object; for that reason, it is proclaimed to be unattached and described as being like space. //96//
When even the slightest difference in nature arises for one who lacks wisdom,
there is never any lack of attachment; how much less, then, could there be the removal of veils?

When even a minute point of dissimilarity—whether external or internal—is produced or brought forth in others who are proponents of other views, those who are unwise and undiscriminating remain unattached; yet their state of non-attachment never truly exists. How much less, then, can it be said that there is freedom from obscuration or the destruction of bondage? //97//
If it is asserted by those who claim that there is no removal of obscuration for these [dharmas] that obscuration is accepted within their own established doctrine,
we reply: "No."
All phenomena are unobstructed and pure by nature;
they were enlightened from the beginning and thus liberated. Therefore, the Leaders are called "Buddhas" because they awaken [to this].
"Unobstructed" (*alabdhāvaraṇāḥ*): those phenomena for which no obstruction—the bondage of ignorance and so forth—has been obtained or attained; the meaning is that they are free from bondage.
They are "naturally immaculate," pure by nature, "awakened from the beginning" (*ādau buddhāḥ*), and likewise "liberated," because their intrinsic nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated.
If this is so, how then is it said that they "awaken"?
The "leaders" (nāyakāḥ) are the masters; the meaning is that they possess the nature of the power of awakening (bodhaśaktimat).
Just as the sun, though its nature is eternal light, is said to "shine," or as mountains, though their motion has eternally ceased, are said to "stand eternally," so it is in this case. //98//
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Protector, does not proceed toward phenomena;
all phenomena are likewise [non-proceeding], and this was not spoken by the Buddha. (MandUpK 4.99)

For the knowledge of the Buddha, who perceives the ultimate truth, does not proceed toward other objects among phenomena, being established within phenomena just as radiance is established in the sun;
he is called "Tāyin" because he possesses *tāya*—
the meaning being that he possesses a continuous, uninterrupted [nature] resembling space.

Whether for one possessing worship or for one possessing wisdom, all phenomena—even the self—are likewise like space due to their being identical to gnosis; the meaning is that they do not proceed toward any other object whatsoever.

This refers to what was introduced at the beginning: "by means of gnosis which is like space," and so forth; because the Protector, the Buddha, is like space, his gnosis is also like space, and thus it does not proceed toward any other object whatsoever.

"Likewise, the dharmas" refers to the reality of the Self as Brahman—immovable like space, changeless, partless, eternal, non-dual, unattached, invisible, ungraspable, and beyond hunger and other such needs;
for the Śruti declares: "Indeed, there is no loss of the vision of the Seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
This non-dual ultimate reality, which is devoid of the distinctions between knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, was not spoken by the Buddha.

Although it is said that the refutation of external objects and the conceptualization of mere consciousness constitute proximity to the non-dual reality, the meaning is that this non-dual ultimate reality is to be known only from the Vedāntas. //99//

At the conclusion of the treatise, a salutation is uttered for the purpose of praising the reality of the supreme truth: The unborn, the equanimous, the wise one— difficult to perceive and exceedingly profound.
Having realized the state that is without plurality, we pay homage according to our strength.
It is "difficult to see" (*durdarśa*), meaning that its vision is attained with difficulty;
the sense is that it is hard to comprehend because its reality is free from the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) of "it exists" or "it does not exist.
For this very reason, it is exceedingly profound and difficult for those of unrefined wisdom to enter, like the great ocean.
Having understood—that is, having realized—the unborn, equal, confident, such state which is non-dual and devoid of multiplicity, we, becoming one with that reality, offer salutation to that state;
the meaning is that, although it is beyond all worldly transaction, we bring it within the scope of conventional discourse according to our strength and according to our power. //100//
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Quelling of the Firebrand," in the Commentary on the Gauḍapādīya Āgama-śāstra composed by the venerable Śaṅkara.
Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!
